q: A transistor is a semiconductor device which works as an amplifier.
e: The textbook defines a transistor as a semiconductor device that functions as an amplifier.

q: In 1949, three American physicists Shockley, Bardeen and Brattain invented the transistor.
e: The text explicitly names Shockley, Bardeen, and Brattain as the inventors of the transistor in 1949.

q: A transistor is made of two layers of p- and n-semiconductors.
e: A transistor is made of three layers of p- and n-semiconductors.

q: In a pnp transistor a thin layer of n-semiconductor is sandwiched between two layers of p-semiconductors.
e: This is the exact structural description of a pnp transistor in the textbook.

q: In an npn transistor a thin layer of p-semiconductor is sandwiched between two layers of n-semiconductors.
e: This is the exact structural description of an npn transistor in the textbook.

q: There are three electrodes in a transistor: the emitter (E), the collector (C) and the base (B).
e: The text lists the emitter, collector, and base as the three electrodes attached to the layers.

q: Transistors deteriorate with time faster than vacuum tubes do.
e: Transistors do not deteriorate with time, whereas vacuum tubes do.

q: Transistors waste much less electrical power than vacuum tubes.
e: One of the listed advantages of transistors is that they waste much less electrical power.

q: Transistors require a long warm-up period after switching on.
e: There is no warm-up period after switching on a transistor.

q: Transistors are physically much more robust than vacuum tubes.
e: The textbook notes that transistors are physically much more robust compared to vacuum tubes.

q: In a transistor biasing circuit, the equation relating currents is $I_E = I_C + I_B$.
e: The textbook provides this exact equation for the currents in a transistor biasing circuit.

q: The base of a transistor is so thick that $I_B \approx 0.02 I_E$ and $I_C \approx 0.98 I_E$.
e: The base of a transistor is so thin, not thick, which results in these current proportions.

q: The small base current $I_B$ can control a very large collector current $I_C$.
e: This controlling property is why a transistor can be regarded as a current amplifier.

q: Because of its property, a transistor can be regarded as a voltage amplifier.
e: The textbook states that a transistor can be regarded as a current amplifier and a power amplifier.

q: The resistance of forward-biased emitter junction is small and that of reverse-biased collector junction is large.
e: The text explicitly contrasts the small resistance of the emitter junction with the large resistance of the collector junction.

q: The electrical power in the emitter side is large whereas the power in the collector side is small.
e: The power in the emitter side is small whereas the power in the collector side is large.

q: Therefore, the transistor can be regarded as a power amplifier.
e: Due to the difference in power between the emitter and collector sides, the transistor acts as a power amplifier.

q: The thickness of the base is about $10^{-3}$ cm and the base layer of a transistor is thinner than other two layers.
e: The textbook specifies the base thickness as $10^{-3}$ cm and notes it is the thinnest layer.
